groups.text: Over three sittings you build one program: a quote service.
A client sends a line like seven EURUSD, and within three hundred milliseconds it gets the best price from three providers.
Here it is, finished.
A Netty server reads the line.
A coroutine service asks Northbank, Eastgate and Fjord at once, and the best price goes back with the same id.
You build it from the outside in.
Each part comes from an earlier lesson, named under the diagram.
Sitting one, in Java, is the Netty shell.
One event-loop thread runs every handler on it, so a handler never waits: it hands the future back at once.
The reply is written later, back on the same loop, so the handler's state needs no lock.
Lines are capped at sixty-four bytes, and the loop reads only while the client keeps up and fewer than sixteen requests wait.
Sitting two writes the service in Kotlin.
Three async calls start together, so a request costs the slowest provider, not the sum.
Each call gets the deadline with withTimeoutOrNull, so a late provider just drops out.
In a supervisorScope, a provider that fails, fails alone.
When nobody answers, the last good price goes out, marked stale.
That rule is new here.
And scope.future gives the Java handler its future.
When a client hangs up, cancelling it cancels all three calls.
Sitting three, still Kotlin, holds it up under load.
Each provider gets its own bulkhead, sized from its contract with Little's law.
Only idempotent calls are retried, with jitter.
Fjord's firm quotes are called once.
Northbank's slow tail gets a hedge: a second call after eighty milliseconds, and the first answer wins.
At the door, admission sheds the overflow at once with ERR busy, and shutdown stops everything in order.
All of it rests on one rule.
The event loop never waits.
The waiting happens in coroutines, inside the deadline.
